name: Dune CCG
notes: Command an Imperial House through a web of politics and desert warfare to master the flow of spice and curry favor from the Landsraad to seize control of Arrakis.
overview: The Dune Collectible Card Game was originally released in 1997 as Dune: Eye of the Storm by a partnership of Five Rings Publishing Group and Last Unicorn Games. The license negotiated with the Herbert Estate and Universal Studios was for intellectual property based on the 1984 film Dune directed by David Lynch, but later the license covered all of the Dune novels by Frank Herbert. Wizards of the Coast purchased Five Rings later that year. In 1998, Wizards of the Coast released two more complete sets and more were planned for release in 1998 but the game was cancelled before they were printed.</br></br>Players represent an Imperial House seeking admission to the Landsraad High Council by amassing at least 10 Spice and 10 Favor. During the game competitors deploy Holdings, Personas, Resources, Plans, and Events. Cards are brought into play either by spending Solaris from the House Treasury or through a competitive, multiplayer bidding process called Petitioning for Imperial cards. The overarching economy revolves around the CHOAM Exchange, where the value of Spice fluctuates based on the supply currently in the Guild Hoard. Players interact by initiating Rites such as Dueling, Battle, Arbitration, or Intrigue, utilizing their cards' various talents to vanquish opposing forces and secure political or economic advantages.</br></br>The game was notable for its "Rolling Thunder" release strategy, which can be compared to today’s LCG model. Small expansions of the game, called "Chapters", were released every two months. While intended to keep the pace of collecting exciting, it resulted in high duplicate rates in booster packs and a competitive landscape constantly in flux.

name: World of Warcraft TCG
notes: Lead a legendary champion with a band of allies through epic quests to claim powerful loot and secure your faction's dominance in the battle for Azeroth.
overview:
The World of Warcraft Trading Card Game was published by Upper Deck Entertainment in October 2006, licensed from Blizzard Entertainment to adapt their massively multiplayer online roleplaying game for the tabletop. Players construct decks built around a central hero card — drawn from the game's classes and races — and compete by deploying allies, abilities, equipment, and locations across a resource system tied to quest cards. The game supported two to six players and was designed to be accessible to WoW players unfamiliar with trading card games while offering enough depth for competitive play.

The WoW TCG is best remembered for its Loot card mechanic: a small number of cards in each set contained a printed code redeemable for exclusive in-game items in World of Warcraft itself, including mounts, pets, and cosmetics. The Spectral Tiger, found in the Fires of Outland set, became one of the most sought-after loot cards in any TCG and continues to command high prices on the secondary market. Beyond the loot cards, the game was notable for its painted card art — many pieces commissioned from artists who had worked on the WoW game itself — and for its structured organised play circuit, which ran regional and world championship events throughout the game's lifespan.

Upper Deck Entertainment lost the Blizzard license in early 2010 following a counterfeit card scandal, after which Cryptozoic Entertainment acquired the rights and continued publishing new sets until 2013 when the line was discontinued entirely. No official digital continuation exists. Blizzard launched Hearthstone, a digital-only card game set in the same universe, in 2014, which effectively replaced the WoW TCG in the market. Original print run cards remain the only source of physical product, with sealed booster boxes and loot cards in particular holding significant collector value.

name: Quest for the Grail CCG
publisher: Horizon Games and Stone Ring Games
notes: Build an Arthurian kingdom and lead legendary knights through trials of valor to achieve the Holy Grail and secure your victory.
overview: Quest for the Grail CCG was published by Horizon Games and Stone Ring in 1995. The game is based on Arthurian legend and was released in two editions, Preview and Limited. An expansion set named Knights of the Isle, based on Scottish and Irish elements, was scheduled for release in April 1996 but was later delayed and never released.</br></br>Players construct a Court deck containing Domains, Warriors, and various assignment cards, alongside a separate Quest deck that generates enemy trials. During the game, competitors deploy Domain cards to produce Power, used to pay the continual upkeep costs of their deployed Knights and retainers. Players interact by outfitting their forces with companions, weapons, and vows, then sending them to fight in formal or mortal combat against opposing Warriors and Quests to accumulate a stat called Valor. The game is won either by fulfilling specific alternate conditions on a King card or by having a Knight with at least 12 Valor successfully defeat three consecutive challenges in the ultimate Quest for the Grail. </br></br>The game featured historic artwork from the 1800's and early 1900's, with work by N.C. Wyeth and Howard Pyle. Newly painted artwork for the game is featured as well.

name: Warhammer 40,000 CCG
notes: Command a powerful army and lead elite warriors through brutal sector assaults to conquer battlegrounds and secure your total dominion.
overview: The Warhammer 40,000 Collectible Card Game was released in 2001 by Sabertooth Games; a total of five sets were printed during the game’s run. After its cancellation in 2003, the game’s system was further reiterated in the form of the Horus Heresy CCG and Dark Millennium CCG before Sabertooth Games closed its doors in 2008.</br></br>Players command a deck representing one of several factions in a bid to conquer a planet by securing three out of five sector cards by the end of the fourth turn. Players alternate between attacker and defender roles, deploying Units, Characters, and Fortifications to specific sectors. In combat players draw a four-card command hand and perform battle actions such as shooting, charging, or assaulting, utilizing their cards' Firepower, Speed, and Armor stats. Randomized elements, such as tests and armor saves, are resolved by discarding the top card of the deck and referencing a printed die number rather than rolling physical dice. A sector is successfully captured at the end of a battle by the player who controls the most flag icons on their surviving deployed forces.</br></br>The game was notable for its launch of the Astronomican player rewards program, which allowed players to gain ranks online by logging games, which enabled them to unlock promo cards for mail-in redemption.

name: Lord of the Rings TCG
overview: The Lord of the Rings Trading Card Game was released in 2001 by Decipher, Inc. It is based on Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings film trilogy and the J. R. R. Tolkien novel on which the films were based. Decipher's license to The Lord of the Rings expired on July 30, 2007, after which all official promotion and distribution of the game stopped.</br></br>Players use custom decks split evenly between "Free Peoples" and "Shadow" cards, alternating roles depending on whose turn it is. As the active Free Peoples player, your objective is to guide your Fellowship across nine sites to destroy the One Ring, using companion characters to defend your Ring-bearer from harm. Simultaneously, your opponents act as the Shadow players, deploying monster minions to attack your Fellowship, inflict wounds, or add "burdens" that slowly corrupt your Ring-bearer's resistance. The game is driven by a unique risk-and-reward resource system called the "twilight pool," where the cost of every card the Free Peoples player plays is added to a shared pool that the Shadow players then spend to fund their attacks. Ultimately, you win the game by being the first to safely navigate your Fellowship to the ninth site, being the last surviving player, or successfully killing or corrupting your opponents' Ring-bearers.</br></br>The game featured stills taken from the films. In 2004 Weta Workshop produced artwork depicting characters and items from the novel absent from the films for use on cards. The game also had an online version that maintained identical gameplay as well as a market economy, its servers closed in June 2010.

name: Harry Potter TCG
overview: The Harry Potter Trading Card Game is a collectible card game based in the world of the Harry Potter novels. Created by Wizards of the Coast in August 2001 the game released four expansion sets, with the final expansion released in 2002, after which Wizards of the Coast discontinued the game.</br></br>Players construct a deck to lead a specific starting Witch or Wizard Character through a head-to-head magical duel. The core gameplay revolves around a fixed 2 actions each turn where you can play Lesson cards to generate Power, cast single-use Spells, play Creatures, and utilize Items, Locations, or Adventures. Cards were separated into five distinct classes or colors: Charms, Potions, Transfiguration, Magical Creatures and Quidditch. Every point of damage dealt discards a card from your opponent's deck, to win the game, you must force your opponent to run out of cards.</br></br>The game featured original artwork and at one point in 2001 was considered the best selling game in the US.

name: Age of Empires ECG
overview: Age of Empires: Expandable Card Game is a trading card game by Journeyman Press. Originally released in 2000, the game was based on the Ensemble Studios computer game, Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings. Due to the bankruptcy of Journeyman Press in 2001, only the base set and the first expansion were published.</br></br>Players construct a custom, era-divided deck to lead a specific faction through four historical Ages, from the Dark Age to the Imperial Age. The core gameplay revolves around managing a multi-phase turn where you allocate Villagers to collect resources, construct Building cards, research Technologies, and deploy military Unit cards. You use these forces to maneuver across the board and attack your opponent's village while upgrading your own civilization's capabilities. To win the game, you must complete one of several distinct victory conditions: achieve military conquest by destroying your opponent's Town Centers or Villagers, secure a religious victory by collecting and protecting five Relics in a Monastery, or reach the final age to build and defend a Wonder for six turns.</br></br>The game featured original artwork. All cards were almost one to one recreations of their video game counterparts.

name: Star Wars CCG
overview: The Star Wars: Customizable Card Game is a customizable card game based on the Star Wars fictional universe. It was created by Decipher, Inc. From its release in December 1995 the game released 11 expansion sets until its discontinuation in December 2001. </br></br>Players construct a custom Light or Dark side deck to lead iconic characters and vehicles through the galaxy. The core gameplay revolves around managing a unique resource system where your deck itself acts as your "Life Force," cycling cards from your deck to deploy Location cards, Characters, Vehicles and more. You use these forces to control contested locations, battle opposing characters, and resolve events like Jedi duels or pod races. The game utilizes a "Destiny draw" mechanic that relies on printed card values rather than dice to resolve chance outcomes. To win the game, you must deplete your opponent's Life Force.</br></br>The game features stills taken from the films. Since 2002, the game has been maintained by the Star Wars CCG Players Committee who have released custom cards and run sanctioned events.
